Visualizing beam search as a tree helps understand how hypotheses are selected and discarded during decoding.
Manual adjustment of attention weights allows users to see how specific source words influence target token probabilities.
Automatic adjustment of attention weights to maximize output probability can make attention alignments more interpretable.
The tool enables exploration of hypotheses not covered by beam search by manually expanding nodes.
Attention weights in NMT may not always look like clear alignments due to language ordering differences, but adjustment can clarify them.
papers.abstract: While neural machine translation (NMT) provides high-quality translation, it is still hard to interpret and analyze its behavior. We present an interactive interface for visualizing and intervening behavior of NMT, specifically concentrating on the behavior of beam search mechanism and attention component. The tool (1) visualizes search tree and attention and (2) provides interface to adjust search tree and attention weight (manually or automatically) at real-time. We show the tool help users understand NMT in various ways.

papers.title: Change of Thought: Adaptive Test-Time Computation
papers.research_question: How can we boost the expressive power of encoder Transformers without resorting to token-level autoregression?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the SELF-Transformer, an encoder layer that iteratively refines its own attention weights to a fixed point, enabling adaptive test-time computation and improving performance without increasing parameter count.
papers.conclusion: SELF-Transformer recovers much of the expressive power of iterative reasoning while preserving the simplicity of pure encoder architectures, demonstrating substantial benefits from input-adaptive alignment at test time.
papers.key_findings:
SELF-Transformer achieves up to 20% accuracy gains on encoder-style benchmarks without increasing parameter count.
On the induction head task, SELF-Transformer achieves 91.1% accuracy compared to 63.1% for a standard Transformer.
On language benchmarks (GLUE, SQuAD, WikiText2), SELF-Transformer outperforms baseline models like BERT-base and RoBERTa-base.
On image classification (ImageNet-1K), SELF-ViT achieves 86.3% top-1 accuracy, outperforming ViT and EfficientNet-B7.
On vision-language tasks, SELF-VLTransformer achieves competitive performance on VQA and retrieval tasks.
papers.limitation:
Computational overhead can arise if the fixed-point iteration requires a high number of steps.
Need for further investigation on generalization capabilities and scaling properties across a wider array of complex tasks, deeper architectures, and longer sequences.
The current implementation does not directly return the iteration count for incorporating an explicit ponder cost for regularization.
future_direction: Adaptation and integration of SELF attention into Large Language Models (LLMs).
Development of more computationally efficient fixed-point solvers and advanced convergence control strategies.
Moving towards explicit and learnable pondering schemes and deeper theoretical understanding of the iterative process.
papers.abstract: Transformers evaluated in a single, fixed-depth pass are provably limited in expressive power to the constant-depth circuit class TC0. Running a Transformer autoregressively removes that ceiling -- first in next-token prediction and, more recently, in chain-of-thought reasoning. Both regimes rely on feedback loops that decode internal states into tokens only to re-encode them in subsequent steps. While this "thinking aloud" mirrors human reasoning, biological brains iterate without externalising intermediate states as language. To boost the expressive power of encoder Transformers without resorting to token-level autoregression, we introduce the SELF-Transformer: an encoder layer that iteratively refines its own attention weights to a fixed point. Instead of producing -- in one pass -- the alignment matrix that remixes the input sequence, the SELF-Transformer iteratively updates that matrix internally, scaling test-time computation with input difficulty. This adaptivity yields up to 20\% accuracy gains on encoder-style benchmarks without increasing parameter count, demonstrating that input-adaptive alignment at test time offers substantial benefits for only a modest extra compute budget. Self-Transformers thus recover much of the expressive power of iterative reasoning while preserving the simplicity of pure encoder architectures.

papers.title: Seq-VCR: Preventing Collapse in Intermediate Transformer Representations for Enhanced Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does representation collapse in intermediate transformer layers limit reasoning capabilities, and can a regularization technique prevent this collapse to improve performance on complex reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces Seq-VCR, a regularization technique that prevents representation collapse in intermediate transformer layers, and shows that combining it with pause tokens improves reasoning performance without explicit chain-of-thought supervision.
papers.conclusion: Intermediate layer representation collapse detrimentally affects the computation of intermediate information essential for solving arithmetic reasoning tasks, and Seq-VCR enhances the model's representation capacity to improve its ability to solve these tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Seq-VCR prevents representation collapse and increases entropy in intermediate transformer layers.
Seq-VCR combined with pause tokens achieves 99.5% exact match accuracy on 5x5 digit multiplication, outperforming same-size models (0%) and GPT-4 with CoT (44%).
Seq-VCR improves performance on arithmetic expression and longest increasing subsequence (LIS) datasets.
Representation collapse is identified as a key factor limiting transformer reasoning capabilities.
Seq-VCR enables models to solve complex reasoning tasks without explicit chain-of-thought supervision.
papers.limitation: Pause tokens share the same embedding, which may limit their effectiveness.
future_direction: Explore the effect of having different embeddings per pause token.
Enhance pre-training with improved representation learning to increase model capabilities.
papers.abstract: Decoder-only Transformers often struggle with complex reasoning tasks, particularly arithmetic reasoning requiring multiple sequential operations. In this work, we identify representation collapse in the model's intermediate layers as a key factor limiting their reasoning capabilities. To address this, we propose Sequential Variance-Covariance Regularization (Seq-VCR), which enhances the entropy of intermediate representations and prevents collapse. Combined with dummy pause tokens as substitutes for chain-of-thought (CoT) tokens, our method significantly improves performance in arithmetic reasoning problems. In the challenging $5 \times 5$ integer multiplication task, our approach achieves $99.5\%$ exact match accuracy, outperforming models of the same size (which yield $0\%$ accuracy) and GPT-4 with five-shot CoT prompting ($44\%$). We also demonstrate superior results on arithmetic expression and longest increasing subsequence (LIS) datasets. Our findings highlight the importance of preventing intermediate layer representation collapse to enhance the reasoning capabilities of Transformers and show that Seq-VCR offers an effective solution without requiring explicit CoT supervision.

papers.title: Knowledge Circuits in Pretrained Transformers
papers.research_question: How do transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative circuits of components such as attention heads and MLPs, and how can these circuits be used to analyze model behaviors and knowledge editing?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces knowledge circuits as a method to uncover how transformers store and express knowledge through collaborative components, and demonstrates their utility in analyzing knowledge editing and model behaviors like hallucinations and in-context learning.
papers.conclusion: Knowledge circuits provide a valuable framework for understanding how transformers store and express knowledge, and can inform the design of better knowledge editing methods.
papers.key_findings:
Knowledge circuits effectively capture knowledge representations, maintaining over 70% of original performance with less than 10% of the graph.
Knowledge is aggregated in early-to-middle layers and enhanced in later layers.
Special components like mover heads and relation heads are critical for information transfer and relational capture.
ROME editing incorporates information at the edited layer, while fine-tuning directly writes knowledge and dominates predictions.
Hallucinations occur when the circuit lacks effective mover heads or they select incorrect information.
papers.limitation:
Coarse granularity of circuits, not capturing fine-grained neuron-level behavior.
Logit lens method may have discrepancies between middle layers and output unembedding matrix.
future_direction: Finer-grained circuit analysis at the neuron level.
Developing more robust techniques to map intermediate representations to outputs (e.g., Attention Lens).
Investigating activation mechanisms of reused heads and polysemanticity.
papers.abstract: The remarkable capabilities of modern large language models are rooted in their vast repositories of knowledge encoded within their parameters, enabling them to perceive the world and engage in reasoning. The inner workings of how these models store knowledge have long been a subject of intense interest and investigation among researchers. To date, most studies have concentrated on isolated components within these models, such as the Multilayer Perceptrons and attention head. In this paper, we delve into the computation graph of the language model to uncover the knowledge circuits that are instrumental in articulating specific knowledge. The experiments, conducted with GPT2 and TinyLLAMA, have allowed us to observe how certain information heads, relation heads, and Multilayer Perceptrons collaboratively encode knowledge within the model. Moreover, we evaluate the impact of current knowledge editing techniques on these knowledge circuits, providing deeper insights into the functioning and constraints of these editing methodologies. Finally, we utilize knowledge circuits to analyze and interpret language model behaviors such as hallucinations and in-context learning. We believe the knowledge circuits hold potential for advancing our understanding of Transformers and guiding the improved design of knowledge editing. Code and data are available in https://github.com/zjunlp/KnowledgeCircuits.

papers.title: Selective Induction Heads: How Transformers Select Causal Structures In Context
papers.research_question: How do transformers select causal structures in context? Specifically, how can they dynamically handle causal structures that change with context?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a framework for selective induction heads, showing how transformers can learn to select the correct causal structure in-context for next-token prediction in interleaved Markov chains.
papers.conclusion: The findings advance the understanding of how transformers select causal structures, providing new insights into their functioning and interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers learn selective induction heads to dynamically select the correct causal structure in-context.
A 3-layer attention-only transformer can implement the selective induction head mechanism.
The constructed transformer matches the performance of trained transformers.
The mechanism asymptotically converges to the maximum likelihood solution.
papers.abstract: Transformers have exhibited exceptional capabilities in sequence modeling tasks, leveraging self-attention and in-context learning. Critical to this success are induction heads, attention circuits that enable copying tokens based on their previous occurrences. In this work, we introduce a novel framework that showcases transformers' ability to dynamically handle causal structures. Existing works rely on Markov Chains to study the formation of induction heads, revealing how transformers capture causal dependencies and learn transition probabilities in-context. However, they rely on a fixed causal structure that fails to capture the complexity of natural languages, where the relationship between tokens dynamically changes with context. To this end, our framework varies the causal structure through interleaved Markov chains with different lags while keeping the transition probabilities fixed. This setting unveils the formation of Selective Induction Heads, a new circuit that endows transformers with the ability to select the correct causal structure in-context. We empirically demonstrate that transformers learn this mechanism to predict the next token by identifying the correct lag and copying the corresponding token from the past. We provide a detailed construction of a 3-layer transformer to implement the selective induction head, and a theoretical analysis proving that this mechanism asymptotically converges to the maximum likelihood solution. Our findings advance the understanding of how transformers select causal structures, providing new insights into their functioning and interpretability.

papers.title: Inner Loop Inference for Pretrained Transformers: Unlocking Latent Capabilities Without Training
papers.research_question: Is it possible to add refinement steps at inference time to improve model performance without changing model parameters?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes inference-time inner looping, a method to extend computation in frozen pretrained Transformers by re-applying a selected block range, leading to modest accuracy gains across benchmarks.
papers.conclusion: Inference-time inner looping offers a lightweight way to expose depth-limited latent computation in off-the-shelf Transformers, further confirming the logits refinement hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Naive inner looping causes distribution shift and performance degradation.
Regularization methods like uniform interpolation enable stable inner looping.
Inner looping yields modest accuracy gains for Gemma models across reasoning benchmarks.
Llama 3-8B is less responsive to inner looping, likely due to its pre-norm architecture.
Visualization of latent trajectories indicates small perturbations that affect final logits.
papers.limitation: The method yields only modest improvements and is less effective on pre-norm architectures like Llama 3-8B.
papers.abstract: Deep Learning architectures, and in particular Transformers, are conventionally viewed as a composition of layers. These layers are actually often obtained as the sum of two contributions: a residual path that copies the input and the output of a Transformer block. As a consequence, the inner representations (i.e. the input of these blocks) can be interpreted as iterative refinement of a propagated latent representation. Under this lens, many works suggest that the inner space is shared across layers, meaning that tokens can be decoded at early stages. Mechanistic interpretability even goes further by conjecturing that some layers act as refinement layers. Following this path, we propose inference-time inner looping, which prolongs refinement in pretrained off-the-shelf language models by repeatedly re-applying a selected block range. Across multiple benchmarks, inner looping yields modest but consistent accuracy improvements. Analyses of the resulting latent trajectories suggest more stable state evolution and continued semantic refinement. Overall, our results suggest that additional refinement can be obtained through simple test-time looping, extending computation in frozen pretrained models.

papers.title: Exploring and Exploiting the Inherent Efficiency within Large Reasoning Models for Self-Guided Efficiency Enhancement
papers.research_question: Can the inherent efficiency within large reasoning models be exploited to reduce overthinking and enhance reasoning efficiency without compromising performance?
papers.core_contribution: This paper reveals that large reasoning models inherently possess untapped efficiency potential, and proposes two self-guided methods—Efficiency Steering (a training-free activation steering technique) and Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL (a reinforcement learning framework)—that significantly reduce reasoning length while preserving or improving task performance.
papers.conclusion: Overthinking in large reasoning models is a controllable behavior embedded in internal representations; the proposed self-guided methods (Efficiency Steering and Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL) successfully enhance reasoning efficiency without external supervision, offering practical directions for building more cost-efficient reasoning systems.
papers.key_findings:
LRMs exhibit inherent efficiency: the shortest correct reasoning paths are often less than half the length of the longest correct ones, indicating substantial untapped efficiency potential.
Efficient and verbose reasoning paths are linearly separable in the model's representation space, with consistent positional shifts across layers and difficulty levels.
Efficiency Steering, a training-free method that injects a single vector direction derived from contrastive reasoning pairs, can controllably modulate reasoning length without compromising accuracy.
Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL, which uses a dynamic reward function balancing correctness and brevity, significantly reduces reasoning length while maintaining or slightly improving accuracy across multiple benchmarks.
Training Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL on simpler mathematical problems (Levels 1-3) leads to efficient reasoning that transfers well to harder problems, suggesting that efficiency priors learned from simple data are effective.
papers.limitation:
Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL is sensitive to optimization steps; beyond 30 steps, efficiency improves but correctness can deteriorate, indicating a trade-off that requires careful tuning.
Training Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL on harder mathematical examples (Levels 4-5) does not yield as favorable efficiency outcomes as training on simpler examples, suggesting that data distribution impacts the method's effectiveness.
future_direction: Further exploration of representational properties of LLMs to build efficiency-aware alignment strategies with minimal external supervision.
Investigating curriculum-aware or simplicity-biased training strategies for self-rewarded efficiency optimization, as simpler problems may provide better efficiency outcomes at lower training cost.
Refining the capabilities that already exist within LRMs for building more efficient and accessible reasoning systems.
papers.abstract: Recent advancements in large reasoning models (LRMs) have significantly enhanced language models' capabilities in complex problem-solving by emulating human-like deliberative thinking. However, these models often exhibit overthinking (i.e., the generation of unnecessarily verbose and redundant content), which hinders efficiency and inflates inference cost. In this work, we explore the representational and behavioral origins of this inefficiency, revealing that LRMs inherently possess the capacity for more concise reasoning. Empirical analyses show that correct reasoning paths vary significantly in length, and the shortest correct responses often suffice, indicating untapped efficiency potential. Exploiting these findings, we propose two lightweight methods to enhance LRM efficiency. First, we introduce Efficiency Steering, a training-free activation steering technique that modulates reasoning behavior via a single direction in the model's representation space. Second, we develop Self-Rewarded Efficiency RL, a reinforcement learning framework that dynamically balances task accuracy and brevity by rewarding concise correct solutions. Extensive experiments on seven LRM backbones across multiple mathematical reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that our methods significantly reduce reasoning length while preserving or improving task performance. Our results highlight that reasoning efficiency can be improved by leveraging and guiding the intrinsic capabilities of existing models in a self-guided manner.

papers.title: Are Transformers Able to Reason by Connecting Separated Knowledge in Training Data?
papers.research_question: When and how can transformers perform compositional reasoning by connecting fragmented knowledge, and what internal mechanisms enable this ability?
papers.core_contribution: Transformers can perform compositional reasoning on the FTCT task via few-shot chain-of-thought prompting, enabled by induction heads and attention assignment, with emergence depending on model complexity and training-testing similarity.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can reason by connecting separated knowledge when provided with few-shot chain-of-thought prompts, and this ability is facilitated by induction heads and attention assignment mechanisms.
papers.key_findings:
Few-shot chain-of-thought prompting enables transformers to perform compositional reasoning by revealing correct vertices order.
Compositional reasoning emerges when the relative knowledge ratio (training child chain length to testing chain length) exceeds 0.3.
Multi-layer attention mechanisms (at least 2 layers and 2 heads) are necessary for compositional reasoning.
Transformers learn an underlying program during training, implemented via induction heads for in-context learning and attention assignment for parent retrieving.
The ability to reason compositionally is robust to noise in testing data but limited when intermediate steps are incomplete.
papers.limitation: Transformers trained on FTCT exhibit limited proficiency in reasoning with incomplete intermediate steps.
papers.abstract: Humans exhibit remarkable compositional reasoning by integrating knowledge from various sources. For example, if someone learns ( B = f(A) ) from one source and ( C = g(B) ) from another, they can deduce ( C=g(B)=g(f(A)) ) even without encountering ( ABC ) together, showcasing the generalization ability of human intelligence. In this paper, we introduce a synthetic learning task, "FTCT" (Fragmented at Training, Chained at Testing), to validate the potential of Transformers in replicating this skill and interpret its inner mechanism. In the training phase, data consist of separated knowledge fragments from an overall causal graph. During testing, Transformers must infer complete causal graph traces by integrating these fragments. Our findings demonstrate that few-shot Chain-of-Thought prompting enables Transformers to perform compositional reasoning on FTCT by revealing correct combinations of fragments, even if such combinations were absent in the training data. Furthermore, the emergence of compositional reasoning ability is strongly correlated with the model complexity and training-testing data similarity. We propose, both theoretically and empirically, that Transformers learn an underlying generalizable program from training, enabling effective compositional reasoning during testing.

papers.title: Anatomy of an Idiom: Tracing Non-Compositionality in Language Models
papers.research_question: What mechanisms do transformers use to process and make sense of natural language, specifically focusing on the processing of non-compositional idiomatic expressions?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces a modified path patching algorithm for circuit discovery and uses it to identify specialized 'Idiom Heads' and a mechanism called 'augmented reception' in transformer models processing idioms, revealing how they balance computational efficiency and robustness.
papers.conclusion: The findings demonstrate that transformers process idioms in early layers with a sequential structure, identify specialized Idiom Heads, and reveal augmented reception as a mechanism for efficient attention, providing insights into non-compositional language processing.
papers.key_findings:
Idioms acquire their non-compositional (figurative) meaning in early layers (0-5) of the network, with a two-phase structure: cross-token attention in layers 0-2 followed by semantic integration in layers 3-5.
Specific attention heads ('Idiom Heads') consistently activate across multiple idioms, suggesting functional specialization for non-compositional language processing.
Each idiom employs a distinct direction in Query-Key space rather than a universal 'idiom direction'.
Early processing of idiom tokens creates 'augmented reception,' enhancing the receptivity of later attention heads to idiom-specific tokens, which is a mechanism for efficient attention allocation.
Most idiomatic processing occurs on the final token of the expression, deferring computation until all necessary context is available.
papers.limitation:
The analysis focuses on English idioms in a single model architecture (Gemma 2–2B).
Threshold determination for circuit discovery introduces subjective elements.
future_direction: Broader study of more idioms in multiple languages and transformer models to confirm generality.
Investigate whether similar patterns occur for other non-compositional phenomena, like grammatical constructions.
Further examples and investigation into augmented reception to deepen understanding of transformer information processing.
papers.abstract: We investigate the processing of idiomatic expressions in transformer-based language models using a novel set of techniques for circuit discovery and analysis. First discovering circuits via a modified path patching algorithm, we find that idiom processing exhibits distinct computational patterns. We identify and investigate ``Idiom Heads,'' attention heads that frequently activate across different idioms, as well as enhanced attention between idiom tokens due to earlier processing, which we term ``augmented reception.'' We analyze these phenomena and the general features of the discovered circuits as mechanisms by which transformers balance computational efficiency and robustness. Finally, these findings provide insights into how transformers handle non-compositional language and suggest pathways for understanding the processing of more complex grammatical constructions.

papers.title: How does GPT-2 compute greater-than?: Interpreting mathematical abilities in a pre-trained language model
papers.research_question: How does GPT-2 compute the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task?
papers.core_contribution: Identifies and explains a circuit in GPT-2 small responsible for computing the greater-than operation in a year-span prediction task, showing it activates across diverse contexts.
papers.conclusion: The study provides a detailed circuit-level explanation of a mathematical ability in a pre-trained LM, laying groundwork for future work on memorization and generalization in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A circuit consisting of specific attention heads and MLPs (8-11) is responsible for the greater-than computation.
Attention heads identify the start year YY and communicate it to downstream MLPs.
MLPs 9, 10, and 11 compute the greater-than operation, with MLP 10 playing a central role.
The circuit generalizes to other tasks requiring greater-than but also incorrectly activates in some contexts (e.g., less-than tasks).
The mechanism is more complex than simple memorization but does not reflect full mathematical generalization.
papers.limitation:
Limited by the small size of the model (GPT-2 small) and the simple phenomenon studied.
The study is model-centric; data-driven interpretability techniques would strengthen the work.
future_direction: Studying circuit performance across more diverse tasks to better measure generalization.
Studying larger models to confirm if the results hold.
papers.abstract: Pre-trained language models can be surprisingly adept at tasks they were not explicitly trained on, but how they implement these capabilities is poorly understood. In this paper, we investigate the basic mathematical abilities often acquired by pre-trained language models. Concretely, we use mechanistic interpretability techniques to explain the (limited) mathematical abilities of GPT-2 small. As a case study, we examine its ability to take in sentences such as "The war lasted from the year 1732 to the year 17", and predict valid two-digit end years (years > 32). We first identify a circuit, a small subset of GPT-2 small's computational graph that computes this task's output. Then, we explain the role of each circuit component, showing that GPT-2 small's final multi-layer perceptrons boost the probability of end years greater than the start year. Finally, we find related tasks that activate our circuit. Our results suggest that GPT-2 small computes greater-than using a complex but general mechanism that activates across diverse contexts.

papers.title: Uncovering Intermediate Variables in Transformers using Circuit Probing
papers.research_question: How can we automatically uncover low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces circuit probing, a method that combines probing and causal analysis to automatically uncover circuits computing hypothesized intermediate variables in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Circuit probing provides a unified approach for a variety of analyses, combining and extending the capabilities of existing methods for interpretability.
papers.key_findings:
Circuit probing can decipher the algorithms learned by models on simple arithmetic tasks.
Circuit probing reveals modular structure within a model, showing that shared and free variables are computed by distinct circuits.
Circuit probing tracks the development of circuits over training, showing circuit formation occurs continuously before generalization.
Circuit probing uncovers circuits responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.
Circuit probing is more faithful to the underlying model computation than linear probing, nonlinear probing, and amnesic probing.
papers.limitation: Neurons are typically polysemantic, so the assumption that a circuit is only causally implicated in computing a single intermediate variable may not hold completely.
papers.abstract: Neural network models have achieved high performance on a wide variety of complex tasks, but the algorithms that they implement are notoriously difficult to interpret. It is often necessary to hypothesize intermediate variables involved in a network's computation in order to understand these algorithms. For example, does a language model depend on particular syntactic properties when generating a sentence? Yet, existing analysis tools make it difficult to test hypotheses of this type. We propose a new analysis technique - circuit probing - that automatically uncovers low-level circuits that compute hypothesized intermediate variables. This enables causal analysis through targeted ablation at the level of model parameters. We apply this method to models trained on simple arithmetic tasks, demonstrating its effectiveness at (1) deciphering the algorithms that models have learned, (2) revealing modular structure within a model, and (3) tracking the development of circuits over training. Across these three experiments we demonstrate that circuit probing combines and extends the capabilities of existing methods, providing one unified approach for a variety of analyses. Finally, we demonstrate circuit probing on a real-world use case: uncovering circuits that are responsible for subject-verb agreement and reflexive anaphora in GPT2-Small and Medium.

papers.title: Interpreting Attention Layer Outputs with Sparse Autoencoders
papers.research_question: Can Sparse Autoencoders be applied to attention layer outputs to obtain interpretable features, and how can this tool be used to better understand attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers?
papers.core_contribution: The paper demonstrates that Sparse Autoencoders can decompose attention layer outputs into sparse, interpretable features, enabling deeper analysis of attention mechanisms and circuits in transformers.
papers.conclusion: Attention Output SAEs are a valuable tool for mechanistic interpretability, allowing for detailed analysis of attention layers and circuits, and should be adopted by the community.
papers.key_findings:
SAEs applied to attention layer outputs yield sparse and interpretable features, with families such as long-range context, short-range context, and induction features.
In GPT-2 Small, at least 90% of attention heads are polysemantic, performing multiple unrelated tasks.
Induction heads can be specialized, with some performing long-prefix induction and others short-prefix induction.
Attention Output SAEs can identify causally relevant features in circuits like the Indirect Object Identification circuit, providing deeper semantic understanding.
The Recursive Direct Feature Attribution (RDFA) technique enables tracing feature contributions through the model.
papers.limitation: The method for interpreting attention heads by looking at the top 10 SAE features may not capture the full role of the head and may miss behaviors that rely on multiple heads (attention head superposition).
papers.abstract: Decomposing model activations into interpretable components is a key open problem in mechanistic interpretability. Sparse autoencoders (SAEs) are a popular method for decomposing the internal activations of trained transformers into sparse, interpretable features, and have been applied to MLP layers and the residual stream. In this work we train SAEs on attention layer outputs and show that also here SAEs find a sparse, interpretable decomposition. We demonstrate this on transformers from several model families and up to 2B parameters. We perform a qualitative study of the features computed by attention layers, and find multiple families: long-range context, short-range context and induction features. We qualitatively study the role of every head in GPT-2 Small, and estimate that at least 90% of the heads are polysemantic, i.e. have multiple unrelated roles. Further, we show that Sparse Autoencoders are a useful tool that enable researchers to explain model behavior in greater detail than prior work. For example, we explore the mystery of why models have so many seemingly redundant induction heads, use SAEs to motivate the hypothesis that some are long-prefix whereas others are short-prefix, and confirm this with more rigorous analysis. We use our SAEs to analyze the computation performed by the Indirect Object Identification circuit (Wang et al.), validating that the SAEs find causally meaningful intermediate variables, and deepening our understanding of the semantics of the circuit. We open-source the trained SAEs and a tool for exploring arbitrary prompts through the lens of Attention Output SAEs.

papers.title: How to think step-by-step: A mechanistic understanding of chain-of-thought reasoning
papers.research_question: How do LLMs internally implement step-by-step reasoning in Chain-of-Thought prompting?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways for step-by-step reasoning, with a functional rift in the middle layers where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior, and answer tokens are collected from both the generated CoT and the question context.
papers.conclusion: CoT reasoning in LLMs is implemented by multiple parallel pathways and a functional rift in the middle layers, with answer tokens collected from various sources.
papers.key_findings:
LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning.
There is a functional rift in the middle layers (around layer 16 in Llama-2 7B) where the model transitions from pretraining prior to in-context prior.
Answer-writing heads appear in the later half of the model (after layer 16).
The model uses both the generated CoT and the question context to generate answers.
Different subtasks (decision, copy, induction) share many of the same attention heads.
papers.limitation:
The study is limited to Llama-2 7B and the PrOntoQA dataset, which may not generalize to other models or real-world reasoning tasks.
The hydra effect and backup circuits in large models make mechanistic interpretation challenging.
future_direction: Extending the analysis to larger models and more diverse reasoning tasks.
papers.abstract: Despite superior reasoning prowess demonstrated by Large Language Models (LLMs) with Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting, a lack of understanding prevails around the internal mechanisms of the models that facilitate CoT generation. This work investigates the neural sub-structures within LLMs that manifest CoT reasoning from a mechanistic point of view. From an analysis of Llama-2 7B applied to multistep reasoning over fictional ontologies, we demonstrate that LLMs deploy multiple parallel pathways of answer generation for step-by-step reasoning. These parallel pathways provide sequential answers from the input question context as well as the generated CoT. We observe a functional rift in the middle layers of the LLM. Token representations in the initial half remain strongly biased towards the pretraining prior, with the in-context prior taking over in the later half. This internal phase shift manifests in different functional components: attention heads that write the answer token appear in the later half, attention heads that move information along ontological relationships appear in the initial half, and so on. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt towards mechanistic investigation of CoT reasoning in LLMs.

papers.title: On the Impact of Fine-Tuning on Chain-of-Thought Reasoning
papers.research_question: How does fine-tuning affect the accuracy and faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning in LLMs, and does it compromise general reasoning capabilities?
papers.core_contribution: Fine-tuning LLMs, especially smaller ones, reduces the accuracy and faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning, with more pronounced negative effects on math tasks.
papers.conclusion: Fine-tuning LLMs, particularly smaller ones, can reduce both the accuracy and faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning, with more severe effects on math tasks.
papers.key_findings:
Fine-tuning generally reduces CoT reasoning accuracy, with the effect being more pronounced in smaller models.
Fine-tuning can compromise the faithfulness of CoT reasoning, as measured by Early Termination, Paraphrasing, and Filler Substitution tests.
The negative impact on faithfulness is more pronounced when fine-tuning on non-reasoning or common-sense reasoning datasets compared to math reasoning datasets.
For smaller models like Llama-3-8b-Instruct, fine-tuning on non-reasoning datasets leads to larger performance drops on out-of-distribution math tasks.
The rank of QLoRA adapters does not significantly change the overall trends in CoT accuracy and faithfulness degradation.
papers.limitation:
The faithfulness of Chain-of-Thought reasoning has not been extensively studied, and the analysis relies on faithfulness metrics that are still in the early stages of development.
Lack of a deeper investigation into how fine-tuning affects the internal mechanisms of LLMs.
future_direction: Using Inference-Time Intervention (ITI) to analyze how fine-tuning modifies activations of reasoning-related attention heads in LLMs.
Exploring the impact of fine-tuning on newer CoT prompting methods and in-context demonstrations.
papers.abstract: Large language models have emerged as powerful tools for general intelligence, showcasing advanced natural language processing capabilities that find applications across diverse domains. Despite their impressive performance, recent studies have highlighted the potential for significant enhancements in LLMs' task-specific performance through fine-tuning strategies like Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF), supervised fine-tuning (SFT), and Quantized Low-Rank Adapters (Q-LoRA) method. However, previous works have shown that while fine-tuning offers significant performance gains, it also leads to challenges such as catastrophic forgetting and privacy and safety risks. To this end, there has been little to no work in \textit{understanding the impact of fine-tuning on the reasoning capabilities of LLMs}. Our research investigates the effect of fine-tuning on the reasoning abilities of LLMs, addressing critical questions regarding the impact of task-specific fine-tuning on overall reasoning capabilities, the influence of fine-tuning on Chain-of-Thought (CoT) reasoning performance, and the implications for the faithfulness of CoT reasonings. By exploring these dimensions, our study shows the impact of fine-tuning on LLM reasoning capabilities, where the faithfulness of CoT reasoning, on average across four datasets, decreases, highlighting potential shifts in internal mechanisms of the LLMs resulting from fine-tuning processes.

papers.title: Towards Best Practices of Activation Patching in Language Models: Metrics and Methods
papers.research_question: How do different methodological choices in activation patching, such as corruption methods and evaluation metrics, affect localization and circuit discovery results in language models?
papers.core_contribution: This paper systematically evaluates hyperparameters in activation patching for language models, finding that choices of corruption methods and metrics significantly affect interpretability results, and provides best practice recommendations.
papers.conclusion: The paper recommends using symmetric token replacement (STR) for in-distribution corruption and logit difference as the evaluation metric for activation patching, highlighting the sensitivity of interpretability results to methodological details.
papers.key_findings:
GN and STR corruption methods lead to inconsistent localization and circuit discovery outcomes.
Probability metric can overlook negative model components that hurt performance, while logit difference is capable of detecting them.
Sliding window patching produces more pronounced localization than summing single-layer patching effects, potentially amplifying weak signals.
GN corruption may put the model off-distribution, breaking internal mechanisms and leading to unreliable interpretability results.
Logit difference is recommended over probability for fine-grained control and detecting negative modules.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability seeks to understand the internal mechanisms of machine learning models, where localization -- identifying the important model components -- is a key step. Activation patching, also known as causal tracing or interchange intervention, is a standard technique for this task (Vig et al., 2020), but the literature contains many variants with little consensus on the choice of hyperparameters or methodology. In this work, we systematically examine the impact of methodological details in activation patching, including evaluation metrics and corruption methods. In several settings of localization and circuit discovery in language models, we find that varying these hyperparameters could lead to disparate interpretability results. Backed by empirical observations, we give conceptual arguments for why certain metrics or methods may be preferred. Finally, we provide recommendations for the best practices of activation patching going forwards.

papers.title: SpiralFormer: Looped Transformers Can Learn Hierarchical Dependencies via Multi-Resolution Recursion
papers.research_question: Can looped transformers learn hierarchical dependencies via multi-resolution recursion?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces multi-resolution recursion for looped Transformers, enabling hierarchical dependency learning and improving parameter and compute efficiency.
papers.conclusion: Multi-resolution recursion is an effective architectural primitive for looped Transformers, enabling hierarchical dependency learning and efficiency gains.
papers.key_findings:
SpiralFormer achieves better parameter and compute efficiency than both looped and non-looped baselines across model scales.
Multi-resolution recursion enables looped Transformers to learn hierarchical dependencies, as evidenced by attention statistics shifts across loops.
Attention becomes more selective and local refinement strengthens as resolution increases in the coarse-to-fine schedule.
papers.limitation: The no-overlap (parallel) regime reduces quality compared to the overlap regime, though it offers inference-time parallelism.
future_direction: Closing the quality gap in the no-overlap regime while retaining parallelism.
Systems optimization for SpiralFormer deployments to exploit inference-time parallelism.
papers.abstract: Recursive (looped) Transformers decouple computational depth from parameter depth by repeatedly applying shared layers, providing an explicit architectural primitive for iterative refinement and latent reasoning. However, early looped Transformers often underperform non-recursive baselines of equal compute. While recent literature has introduced more effective recursion mechanisms to mitigate this gap, existing architectures still operate at a fixed, full-token resolution, neglecting the potential efficiency of computing over compressed latent representations. In this paper, we propose SpiralFormer, a looped Transformer that executes recurrence under a multi-resolution recursion schedule. We provide probing evidence that multi-resolution recursion enables the model to learn hierarchical dependencies by inducing iteration-wise functional specialization across different scales. Empirically, SpiralFormer achieves better parameter and compute efficiency than both looped and non-looped baselines across model scales from 160M to 1.4B, establishing sequence resolution as a potential axis for scaling recursive architectures.

papers.title: Emergence of Minimal Circuits for Indirect Object Identification in Attention-Only Transformers
papers.research_question: How do minimal circuits for indirect object identification emerge in attention-only transformers trained from scratch on a symbolic task?
papers.core_contribution: Demonstrates that task-constrained training induces highly interpretable, minimal circuits for indirect object identification in attention-only transformers.
papers.conclusion: Task-constrained training can produce parsimonious and interpretable circuits, offering insight into computational motifs underlying reasoning in larger models.
papers.key_findings:
A single-layer, two-head attention-only transformer achieves perfect accuracy on the symbolic IOI task.
The two heads specialize into additive and contrastive subcircuits that jointly implement IOI resolution.
A two-layer, one-head model achieves similar performance through composition across layers via query-value interactions.
Positional embeddings improve accuracy and interpretability but are not strictly necessary for the task.
The circuits in task-constrained models are more parsimonious than those in broadly pre-trained models.
papers.abstract: Mechanistic interpretability aims to reverse-engineer large language models (LLMs) into human-understandable computational circuits. However, the complexity of pretrained models often obscures the minimal mechanisms required for specific reasoning tasks. In this work, we train small, attention-only transformers from scratch on a symbolic version of the Indirect Object Identification (IOI) task -- a benchmark for studying coreference -- like reasoning in transformers. Surprisingly, a single-layer model with only two attention heads achieves perfect IOI accuracy, despite lacking MLPs and normalization layers. Through residual stream decomposition, spectral analysis, and embedding interventions, we find that the two heads specialize into additive and contrastive subcircuits that jointly implement IOI resolution. Furthermore, we show that a two-layer, one-head model achieves similar performance by composing information across layers through query-value interactions. These results demonstrate that task-specific training induces highly interpretable, minimal circuits, offering a controlled testbed for probing the computational foundations of transformer reasoning.

papers.title: Towards Revealing the Mystery behind Chain of Thought: A Theoretical Perspective
papers.research_question: What are the underlying mechanisms behind Chain-of-Thought (CoT) prompting and how does it unlock the potential of Large Language Models (LLMs) for mathematical and reasoning tasks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper theoretically proves that bounded-depth Transformers without Chain-of-Thought (CoT) require super-polynomial size to solve basic mathematical tasks, while constant-size autoregressive Transformers with CoT can solve them, and extends this to show CoT enables solving dynamic programming problems.
papers.conclusion: Chain-of-Thought is the key to unlocking the reasoning capabilities of autoregressive Transformers, both theoretically and empirically, by allowing step-by-step generation that overcomes the expressivity limitations of bounded-depth models.
papers.key_findings:
Bounded-depth log-precision Transformers of polynomial size cannot directly solve arithmetic and linear equation tasks unless the model size grows super-polynomially with input length.
Autoregressive Transformers of constant depth and size can generate correct CoT solutions for arithmetic and linear equation tasks.
LLMs with CoT can solve a general class of decision-making problems formulated as dynamic programming.
Experimental results show Transformers fail to directly predict answers but consistently learn to generate correct step-by-step CoT solutions given sufficient demonstrations.
CoT increases the effective depth of the Transformer circuit, allowing it to solve problems beyond the TC0 complexity class.
papers.abstract: Recent studies have discovered that Chain-of-Thought prompting (CoT) can dramatically improve the performance of Large Language Models (LLMs), particularly when dealing with complex tasks involving mathematics or reasoning. Despite the enormous empirical success, the underlying mechanisms behind CoT and how it unlocks the potential of LLMs remain elusive. In this paper, we take a first step towards theoretically answering these questions. Specifically, we examine the expressivity of LLMs with CoT in solving fundamental mathematical and decision-making problems. By using circuit complexity theory, we first give impossibility results showing that bounded-depth Transformers are unable to directly produce correct answers for basic arithmetic/equation tasks unless the model size grows super-polynomially with respect to the input length. In contrast, we then prove by construction that autoregressive Transformers of constant size suffice to solve both tasks by generating CoT derivations using a commonly used math language format. Moreover, we show LLMs with CoT can handle a general class of decision-making problems known as Dynamic Programming, thus justifying its power in tackling complex real-world tasks. Finally, an extensive set of experiments show that, while Transformers always fail to directly predict the answers, they can consistently learn to generate correct solutions step-by-step given sufficient CoT demonstrations.

papers.title: Mechanism and Emergence of Stacked Attention Heads in Multi-Layer Transformers
papers.research_question: What tasks require transformers of a specific depth? Can large language models solve such tasks without fine-tuning? What mechanism do transformers use to solve the task? How does this mechanism emerge during training?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces the retrieval problem, a task requiring a minimum number of transformer layers, and uncovers that transformers solve it using stacked attention heads (retrieval heads) which emerge gradually via an implicit curriculum.
papers.conclusion: The work introduces the retrieval problem, shows it requires a certain number of layers, and finds transformers solve it using a mechanism resembling an induction head that emerges gradually with the help of an implicit curriculum.
papers.key_findings:
The retrieval problem requires a minimum number of transformer layers that grows logarithmically with the number of retrieval steps.
Large language models can solve the retrieval problem without any specific fine-tuning.
Transformers solve the retrieval problem using stacked attention heads that resemble induction heads.
Retrieval heads emerge gradually during training, one head at a time, guided by an implicit curriculum.
The implicit curriculum is essential for successful learning of the retrieval problem.
papers.limitation:
The analysis of transformers trained on a minimal formulation of the retrieval problem might not generalize perfectly to large language models.
The paper does not provide a full explanation of the training dynamics of transformers on the retrieval problem.
future_direction: Further research is needed to fully understand the multi-layered circuits learned by large language models and the training dynamics that enable their learning.
papers.abstract: In this paper, I introduce the retrieval problem, a simple yet common reasoning task that can be solved only by transformers with a minimum number of layers, which grows logarithmically with the input size. I empirically show that large language models can solve the task under different prompting formulations without any fine-tuning. To understand how transformers solve the retrieval problem, I train several transformers on a minimal formulation. Successful learning occurs only under the presence of an implicit curriculum. I uncover the learned mechanisms by studying the attention maps in the trained transformers. I also study the training process, uncovering that attention heads always emerge in a specific sequence guided by the implicit curriculum.

papers.title: Simple Recursive Model: Simplified, Single-State Reasoning with Skip Connections
papers.research_question: Does the dual-state structure in hierarchical reasoning models (HRM/TRM) provide benefit through hierarchical separation or through access to information across timescales? Can skip connections achieve similar performance with a simpler architecture?
papers.core_contribution: The paper shows that the benefit of hierarchical reasoning models comes from accessing information across timescales, which can be achieved with skip connections in a simpler single-state architecture, as demonstrated by the Simple Recursive Model (SRM).
papers.conclusion: SRM simplifies hierarchical architectures by using skip connections instead of dual states, achieving comparable performance, and the refinement learning framework provides a unified perspective on various models.
papers.key_findings:
Skip connections with transformed states (f(z) or f_new(z)) in SRM achieve performance comparable to the dual-state TRM baseline on Sudoku solving.
Truncated backpropagation with very small truncation lengths (T=2 or T=3) is sufficient for effective training and sometimes performs better than longer truncation windows.
SRM without skip connections performs poorly, indicating that access to earlier information is necessary for reasoning tasks.
papers.limitation: Only evaluated on Sudoku solving tasks, so generalizability to other reasoning tasks is unknown.
future_direction: Investigate whether the same simplifications hold for other reasoning tasks, such as mathematical problem solving or logical reasoning.
Explore whether other forms of skip connections could further improve performance.
papers.abstract: <title>Abstract</title> Hierarchical Reasoning Models (HRM) and their variants (TRM) have shown impressive performance on a variety of reasoning tasks. These models maintain two separate states $z_L$ and $z_H$ that are designed to capture low-level and high-level representations for reasoning. However, the necessity of this dual-state strcuture remains unclear. We conjecture that the benefit of $z_H$ stems not necessarily from representing any distinct level of information, but rather from providing access to information from earlier timesteps, as $z_H$ is updated less frequently than $z_L$. To test this, we propose Simple Recursive Model (SRM): a model that maintains only a single state $z$ and adopts skip connections to earlier timesteps in replacement of the second-level state $z_H$. This approach eliminates the complicated nested loops in HRM/TRM that alternate between $z_L$ and $z_H$, leading to a more straightforward and parsimonious architecture. Through experiments on the Sudoku task, we demonstrate that the single-state SRM can achieve comparable performance to the TRM baseline. Our results suggest that the key benefit of HRM/TRM is not necessarily hierarchical state separation, but may come from the ability to access information across different timescales. Such ability can be equivalently achieved through other mechanisms such as skip connections, opening up new avenues for designing simpler and more efficient reasoning models. Code available at: https://github.com/liaoq/SimpleRecursiveModel

papers.title: Mechanisms of Symbol Processing for In-Context Learning in Transformer Networks
papers.research_question: How can transformer networks perform abstract, semantics-free symbol processing through in-context learning, and can insights from symbolic AI and transformer architecture help design such networks?
papers.core_contribution: The paper introduces the Transformer Production Framework (TPF), which shows how transformer networks can be programmed to perform semantics-free symbol processing through in-context learning, and demonstrates that such transformers are Turing-complete.
papers.conclusion: Transformers can perform abstract symbol processing through mechanisms akin to production systems, and the TPF offers a path to more interpretable and capable transformers.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers can implement production system programs via attention mechanisms, enabling semantics-free symbol processing.
The Discrete-Attention-only Transformer (DAT) can achieve 100% accuracy on the Templatic Generation Task.
The Production System Language (PSL) is Turing-complete, so transformers can be universal computers.
The framework provides a fully interpretable transformer by construction.
The work suggests that transformers' symbol processing abilities may arise from mechanisms similar to induction heads and state-variable encodings.
papers.limitation: The work addresses computability, not learnability, by transformer networks.
future_direction: Combining the new attention heads with traditional attention heads in a new type of transformer.
Testing whether trained language models use similar mechanisms for symbol processing.
Extending compositionality further.
papers.abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive abilities in symbol processing through in-context learning (ICL). This success flies in the face of decades of critiques asserting that artificial neural networks cannot master abstract symbol manipulation. We seek to understand the mechanisms that can enable robust symbol processing in transformer networks, illuminating both the unanticipated success, and the significant limitations, of transformers in symbol processing. Borrowing insights from symbolic AI and cognitive science on the power of Production System architectures, we develop a high-level Production System Language, PSL, that allows us to write symbolic programs to do complex, abstract symbol processing, and create compilers that precisely implement PSL programs in transformer networks which are, by construction, 100% mechanistically interpretable. The work is driven by study of a purely abstract (semantics-free) symbolic task that we develop, Templatic Generation (TGT). Although developed through study of TGT, PSL is, we demonstrate, highly general: it is Turing Universal. The new type of transformer architecture that we compile from PSL programs suggests a number of paths for enhancing transformers' capabilities at symbol processing. We note, however, that the work we report addresses computability, and not learnability, by transformer networks. Note: The first section provides an extended synopsis of the entire paper.

papers.title: Implicit Reasoning in Transformers is Reasoning through Shortcuts
papers.research_question: Why does advanced reasoning capability fail to emerge in implicit reasoning? How do language models perform implicit reasoning in multi-step mathematical tasks?
papers.core_contribution: Language models acquire implicit reasoning through shortcut learning, which enables strong performance on tasks with similar patterns but lacks generalization, especially in the 'Variable as Subtrahend Plight'.
papers.conclusion: Language models rely on shortcuts for implicit reasoning, which only work when training data aligns with a specific pattern, and they struggle when true reasoning is required.
papers.key_findings:
Language models can perform step-by-step implicit reasoning and generalize to longer steps when trained on fixed-pattern data.
When trained on unfixed-pattern data, models overfit to shortcuts and fail to generalize, particularly in cases with variables as subtrahends.
State-of-the-art LLMs also rely on shortcuts for implicit reasoning and struggle with variable subtrahends, indicating the generality of the shortcut learning phenomenon.
papers.limitation:
Only two fundamental arithmetic operators are used, limiting the scope of mathematical reasoning studied.
Evaluation of LLMs may be inflated if they were exposed to similar synthetic tasks during training.
future_direction: Expand to include a broader range of mathematical operators.
Explore reasoning beyond arithmetic problems, e.g., commonsense reasoning.
papers.abstract: Test-time compute is emerging as a new paradigm for enhancing language models' complex multi-step reasoning capabilities, as demonstrated by the success of OpenAI's o1 and o3, as well as DeepSeek's R1. Compared to explicit reasoning in test-time compute, implicit reasoning is more inference-efficient, requiring fewer generated tokens. However, why does the advanced reasoning capability fail to emerge in the implicit reasoning style? In this work, we train GPT-2 from scratch on a curated multi-step mathematical reasoning dataset and conduct analytical experiments to investigate how language models perform implicit reasoning in multi-step tasks. Our findings reveal: 1) Language models can perform step-by-step reasoning and achieve high accuracy in both in-domain and out-of-domain tests via implicit reasoning. However, this capability only emerges when trained on fixed-pattern data. 2) Conversely, implicit reasoning abilities emerging from training on unfixed-pattern data tend to overfit a specific pattern and fail to generalize further. Notably, this limitation is also observed in state-of-the-art large language models. These findings suggest that language models acquire implicit reasoning through shortcut learning, enabling strong performance on tasks with similar patterns while lacking generalization.

papers.title: Arithmetic Without Algorithms: Language Models Solve Math With a Bag of Heuristics
papers.research_question: Do large language models (LLMs) solve arithmetic reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms or by memorizing training data?
papers.core_contribution: LLMs solve arithmetic tasks by combining a sparse set of heuristic neurons, each implementing simple patterns, forming a 'bag of heuristics' rather than using a robust algorithm or memorization.
papers.conclusion: LLMs implement a bag of heuristics—a combination of many memorized rules—to perform arithmetic reasoning, rather than using robust algorithms or pure memorization.
papers.key_findings:
A sparse subset of MLP neurons in the arithmetic circuit implements simple heuristics for arithmetic.
Each heuristic neuron activates for specific input patterns and promotes corresponding answer tokens.
The combination of these heuristic neurons (a bag of heuristics) explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts.
This mechanism emerges early in training and persists as the main source of arithmetic accuracy.
The bag of heuristics fails to generalize perfectly, leading to errors when prompts lack sufficient associated heuristics or when heuristics have imperfect recall.
papers.limitation:
Human bias in defining heuristic types, as abstractions are based on human-identifiable definitions.
Analysis focuses on LLMs that tokenize multi-digit numbers as single tokens, which may not generalize to models with single-digit tokenization.
future_direction: Developing methods to identify heuristic abstractions without human bias.
Investigating if regularization can improve the bag of heuristics mechanism.
Exploring fundamental changes to training and architectures to improve mathematical abilities.
papers.abstract: Do large language models (LLMs) solve reasoning tasks by learning robust generalizable algorithms, or do they memorize training data? To investigate this question, we use arithmetic reasoning as a representative task. Using causal analysis, we identify a subset of the model (a circuit) that explains most of the model's behavior for basic arithmetic logic and examine its functionality. By zooming in on the level of individual circuit neurons, we discover a sparse set of important neurons that implement simple heuristics. Each heuristic identifies a numerical input pattern and outputs corresponding answers. We hypothesize that the combination of these heuristic neurons is the mechanism used to produce correct arithmetic answers. To test this, we categorize each neuron into several heuristic types-such as neurons that activate when an operand falls within a certain range-and find that the unordered combination of these heuristic types is the mechanism that explains most of the model's accuracy on arithmetic prompts. Finally, we demonstrate that this mechanism appears as the main source of arithmetic accuracy early in training. Overall, our experimental results across several LLMs show that LLMs perform arithmetic using neither robust algorithms nor memorization; rather, they rely on a "bag of heuristics".

papers.title: KV Cache Steering for Controlling Frozen LLMs
papers.research_question: Can we develop lightweight, post-training interventions to unlock and steer inherent reasoning processes in language models, specifically via a one-shot modification of the key-value cache?
papers.core_contribution: Introduces cache steering, a one-shot method for steering language model behavior by modifying the key-value cache, which is more efficient and stable than continuous activation steering and does not require fine-tuning.
papers.conclusion: Cache steering provides a lightweight, practical mechanism for behavior-level guidance of language models, offering a stable and efficient alternative to activation steering and fine-tuning.
papers.key_findings:
Cache steering induces chain-of-thought reasoning in small language models without fine-tuning or prompt modifications.
The method improves reasoning structure and task performance on multiple benchmarks (GSM8K, ARC-c, CSQA, PIQA).
Cache steering is more computationally efficient and stable to hyperparameters than activation steering.
The technique enables controllable transfer of reasoning styles (e.g., stepwise, causal, analogical) from teacher models.
The method scales to larger models and yields gains on challenging datasets like GPQA and MATH.
papers.limitation:
Further study is needed to assess how well cache steering generalizes across a wider range of large models, domains, and tasks beyond reasoning.
Potential misuse, such as steering toward deceptive, harmful, or biased outputs, remains a concern.
future_direction: Further study to assess generalization across a wider range of large models, domains, and tasks beyond reasoning.
papers.abstract: We propose cache steering, a lightweight method for implicit steering of language models via a one-shot intervention applied directly to the key-value cache. To validate its effectiveness, we apply cache steering to induce chain-of-thought reasoning in small language models. Our approach constructs steering vectors from reasoning traces, obtained either from teacher models (e.g., GPT-4o) or existing human annotations, that shift model behavior toward more explicit, multi-step reasoning without fine-tuning or prompt modifications. Experimental evaluations on diverse reasoning benchmarks demonstrate that cache steering improves both the qualitative structure of model reasoning and quantitative task performance. Additional experiments show that the method also scales to larger models and yields further gains on challenging datasets such as GPQA and MATH. Compared to prior activation steering techniques that require continuous interventions, our one-shot cache steering offers substantial advantages in terms of inference latency, hyperparameter stability, and ease of integration with existing inference APIs. Beyond mere reasoning induction, we show that cache steering enables controllable transfer of reasoning styles (e.g., stepwise, causal, analogical), making it a practical tool for behavior-level guidance of language models.

papers.title: Finding Transformer Circuits with Edge Pruning
papers.research_question: How can we efficiently and accurately discover sparse computational subgraphs (circuits) in transformers that capture specific model behaviors?
papers.core_contribution: Proposes Edge Pruning, an efficient and scalable gradient-based pruning method for automated circuit discovery that finds sparser and more faithful circuits than prior methods.
papers.conclusion: Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability that can shed light on behaviors emerging in large models.
papers.key_findings:
Edge Pruning finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the edges of prior methods while being equally faithful on standard tasks.
The method scales effectively to 100K examples and to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x larger than GPT-2.
It perfectly recovers ground-truth circuits in Tracr-compiled models.
A case study on CodeLlama-13B reveals substantial overlap between circuits for instruction-prompted and in-context learning settings, suggesting shared mechanisms.
papers.limitation:
The method's reliance on providing corrupted examples for interchange ablation.
Potential challenges in converging to very high sparsity regimes.
future_direction: Improving the efficiency and scalability of the method further.
Applying Edge Pruning to more complex tasks and model behaviors.
Exploring the method's applicability to other model architectures.
papers.abstract: The path to interpreting a language model often proceeds via analysis of circuits -- sparse computational subgraphs of the model that capture specific aspects of its behavior. Recent work has automated the task of discovering circuits. Yet, these methods have practical limitations, as they rely either on inefficient search algorithms or inaccurate approximations. In this paper, we frame automated circuit discovery as an optimization problem and propose *Edge Pruning* as an effective and scalable solution. Edge Pruning leverages gradient-based pruning techniques, but instead of removing neurons or components, it prunes the \emph{edges} between components. Our method finds circuits in GPT-2 that use less than half the number of edges compared to circuits found by previous methods while being equally faithful to the full model predictions on standard circuit-finding tasks. Edge Pruning is efficient even with as many as 100K examples, outperforming previous methods in speed and producing substantially better circuits. It also perfectly recovers the ground-truth circuits in two models compiled with Tracr. Thanks to its efficiency, we scale Edge Pruning to CodeLlama-13B, a model over 100x the scale that prior methods operate on. We use this setting for a case study comparing the mechanisms behind instruction prompting and in-context learning. We find two circuits with more than 99.96% sparsity that match the performance of the full model and reveal that the mechanisms in the two settings overlap substantially. Our case study shows that Edge Pruning is a practical and scalable tool for interpretability and sheds light on behaviors that only emerge in large models.

papers.title: Faith and Fate: Limits of Transformers on Compositionality
papers.research_question: What are the limitations of transformer LLMs on compositional tasks, and are their errors incidental or do they signal fundamental limitations?
papers.core_contribution: Transformer LLMs solve compositional tasks via linearized subgraph matching rather than systematic reasoning, and they exhibit exponential error accumulation with increased complexity.
papers.conclusion: Transformers have inherent limitations in solving compositionally complex tasks, and fundamental innovations are needed to address these limitations.
papers.key_findings:
Transformers' accuracy on compositional tasks drops to near zero as task complexity increases.
Fine-tuning on task-specific data leads to near-perfect in-domain performance but poor out-of-domain generalization.
Transformers learn surface patterns (e.g., via relative information gain) rather than underlying algorithms.
Correct predictions correlate with frequency of subgraph patterns in training data, indicating pattern matching.
Error analysis shows propagation errors dominate, indicating failure to compose steps.
papers.limitation: Due to budget constraints, grokking experiments were only conducted on the multiplication task.
future_direction: Using transformers for tasks decomposable into few reasoning steps
Using transformers in combination with planning modules or refinement methods
Fundamental innovations to address limitations
papers.abstract: Transformer large language models (LLMs) have sparked admiration for their exceptional performance on tasks that demand intricate multi-step reasoning. Yet, these models simultaneously show failures on surprisingly trivial problems. This begs the question: Are these errors incidental, or do they signal more substantial limitations? In an attempt to demystify transformer LLMs, we investigate the limits of these models across three representative compositional tasks -- multi-digit multiplication, logic grid puzzles, and a classic dynamic programming problem. These tasks require breaking problems down into sub-steps and synthesizing these steps into a precise answer. We formulate compositional tasks as computation graphs to systematically quantify the level of complexity, and break down reasoning steps into intermediate sub-procedures. Our empirical findings suggest that transformer LLMs solve compositional tasks by reducing multi-step compositional reasoning into linearized subgraph matching, without necessarily developing systematic problem-solving skills. To round off our empirical study, we provide theoretical arguments on abstract multi-step reasoning problems that highlight how autoregressive generations' performance can rapidly decay with\,increased\,task\,complexity.

papers.title: Not All Language Model Features Are One-Dimensionally Linear
papers.research_question: Are some language model representations inherently multi-dimensional, and if so, how are these irreducible multi-dimensional features used in computation?
papers.core_contribution: This paper demonstrates that language models learn irreducible multi-dimensional features (e.g., circular representations for days of the week and months of the year) and provides evidence that these features are the fundamental unit of computation for modular arithmetic tasks.
papers.conclusion: Understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary for a complete mechanistic decomposition of some language model behaviors, challenging the strict one-dimensional linear representation hypothesis.
papers.key_findings:
Sparse autoencoders can automatically discover interpretable multi-dimensional features in language models, such as circular representations for days of the week and months of the year.
These circular features are irreducible according to formal separability and mixture indices, meaning they cannot be decomposed into independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features.
Models like Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B use these exact circular representations when solving modular arithmetic problems involving days and months.
Intervention experiments (subspace patching) show that the circular representations are causally involved in the model's computation for these tasks.
The circular representations respect a continuous notion of time, as shown by interventions with phrases like 'early Monday' and 'late Monday'.
papers.abstract: Recent work has proposed that language models perform computation by manipulating one-dimensional representations of concepts ("features") in activation space. In contrast, we explore whether some language model representations may be inherently multi-dimensional. We begin by developing a rigorous definition of irreducible multi-dimensional features based on whether they can be decomposed into either independent or non-co-occurring lower-dimensional features. Motivated by these definitions, we design a scalable method that uses sparse autoencoders to automatically find multi-dimensional features in GPT-2 and Mistral 7B. These auto-discovered features include strikingly interpretable examples, e.g. circular features representing days of the week and months of the year. We identify tasks where these exact circles are used to solve computational problems involving modular arithmetic in days of the week and months of the year. Next, we provide evidence that these circular features are indeed the fundamental unit of computation in these tasks with intervention experiments on Mistral 7B and Llama 3 8B, and we examine the continuity of the days of the week feature in Mistral 7B. Overall, our work argues that understanding multi-dimensional features is necessary to mechanistically decompose some model behaviors.

papers.title: Constituency Parsing with a Self-Attentive Encoder
papers.research_question: Can replacing an LSTM encoder with a self-attentive architecture improve constituency parsing? How does factoring content and position information in attention affect performance?
papers.core_contribution: Replacing an LSTM encoder with a self-attentive architecture improves constituency parsing accuracy, and explicitly factoring content and position information within the attention mechanism leads to further performance gains.
papers.conclusion: The choice of encoder architecture significantly impacts parser performance, and a factored self-attentive encoder achieves state-of-the-art results, suggesting further research into utterance encoding can benefit parsing and other NLP tasks.
papers.key_findings:
A self-attentive encoder outperforms an LSTM-based encoder for constituency parsing.
Factoring content and position information in the attention mechanism improves parsing accuracy.
Using a character-level LSTM for lexical representation outperforms using part-of-speech tags from an external tagger.
